etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smerten, from Old English *smeortan (“to smart”), from Proto-West Germanic *smertan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną (“to hurt, ache”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with Scots smert, Dutch smarten, German schmerzen, Danish smerte, Swedish smärta.

quote.citation: 1897, Bram Stoker, chapter 21, in Dracula, New York, N.Y.: Modern Library, →OCLC:
quote.text: He moved convulsively, and as he did so, said, "I'll be quiet, Doctor. Tell them to take off the strait waistcoat. I have had a terrible dream, and it has left me so weak that I cannot move. What's wrong with my face? It feels all swollen, and it smarts dreadfully."

quote.citation: 2023 October 12, HarryBlank, “Fire in the Hole”, in SCP Foundation‎[1], archived from the original on 22 May 2024:
quote.text: When the thrashing stopped, Fina used the pipe to roll the first woman's corpse over. She bent down, feeling a curious distance between the sudden serenity in her mind and the actions of her limbs, and beat the flames off the jacket with her bare hands. They were sooty and smarting as she used them to pry the garment off the woman's slack shoulders, and threw it over her own.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause a smart or sting in.

quote.citation: a. 1652, Thomas Adams, Faith’s Encouragement:
quote.text: A goad that  […]  smarts the flesh.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To feel a pungent pain of mind; to feel sharp pain or grief; to be punished severely; to feel the sting of evil.

quote.citation: 1735 January 13 (Gregorian calendar; indicated as 1734), [Alexander] Pope, An Epistle from Mr. Pope, to Dr. Arbuthnot, London:  […]  J[ohn] Wright for Lawton Gilliver […], →OCLC, page 5, lines 81–82:
quote.text: You think this cruel? take it for a rule, / No creature ſmarts ſo little as a Fool.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 11:15:
quote.text: He that is ſurety for a ſtranger ſhall ſmart for it.

quote.citation: 1790, [Ann Radcliffe], chapter XI, in A Sicilian Romance. […], volume II, London:  […]  T[homas] Hookham, […], →OCLC, page 85:
quote.text: Meanvvhile the Abate exulted in ſucceſsful vengeance, and the marquis ſmarted beneath the ſtings of diſappointment.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smert, smart, from Old English smeart (“smarting, smart, painful”), from Proto-Germanic *smartaz (“hurting, aching”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with Scots smert (“painful, smart”), Old Frisian smert (“sharp, painful”).

quote.citation: 1811, [Jane Austen], chapter 19, in Sense and Sensibility […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  C[harles] Roworth, […], and published by T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I always preferred the church, and I still do. But that was not smart enough for my family. They recommended the army. That was a great deal too smart for me.

definitions.definition: (informal) Exhibiting intellectual knowledge, such as that found in books.
(often in combination) Equipped with intelligent behaviour (digital/computer technology).

quote.citation: 2018 December 18, Joe Pinsker, “The Coming Commodification of Life at Home”, in The Atlantic‎[2]:
quote.text: “Imagine this,” says an advertising consultant named Barry Lowenthal. “I’m a smart toaster, and I’m collecting data on how many times the toaster is used.”

definitions.definition: Cleverly shrewd and humorous in a way that may be rude and disrespectful.

quote.citation: 1728, Edward Young, Satire:
quote.text: Who, for the poor renown of being smart / Would leave a sting within a brother's heart?

quote.citation: 1711 October 1 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison; Richard Steele et al.], “THURSDAY, September 20, 1711”, in The Spectator, number 175; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume II, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: I played a sentence or two at my butt, which I thought very smart, when my ill genius, who I verily believed inspired him purely for my destruction, suggested to him such a replyThe spelling has been modernized.

quote.citation: 1860 July 9, Henry David Thoreau, journal entry, from Thoreau's bird-lore, Francis H. Allen (editor), Houghton Mifflin (Boston, 1910), Thoreau on Birds: notes on New England birds from the Journals of Henry David Thoreau, Beacon Press, (Boston, 1993), page 239:

definitions.definition: (Southern US, dated) Intense in feeling; painful. Used usually with the adverb intensifier right.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Georgic 1”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English smerte, from smerten (“to smart”); see above. Cognate with Scots smert, Dutch smart, Low German smart, German Schmerz, Danish smerte, Swedish smärta. More above.

definitions.definition: A sharp, quick, lively pain; a sting.

definitions.definition: Mental pain or suffering; grief; affliction.
